newsitem.title: GERMANY: Publishers face losses over German spelling chaos.
newsitem.headline: Publishers face losses over German spelling chaos.

text.p: Publishers of German schoolbooks said on Wednesday they stood to lose hundreds of millions of marks (dollars) if a controversial reform of the language's notoriously tricky spelling rules founders.

The reform, which has already found its way into the curricula of some German schools but only becomes binding in 2005, was thrown into doubt last month when a regional German court determined it was unlawful.

"Stocks of books already published in the reworked form have a value of some 130 million marks ($69 million) and additional costs related to the conversion amount to 50 million marks," the Federation of Schoolbook Publishers said in a statement.

Publishers had been confidently expecting a windfall to result from the reform, as schools were required to order books adhering to the new rules. Many schools have planned to begin teaching the reform at the start of this academic year.

But opponents of the reform, which among other things simplifies rules on commas and does away with the last vestige of German's old Gothic alphabet, say formal law changes are required before it can be enacted.
Since the July decision of a court in the central state of Hesse banning schools there from teaching the new rules, other states have insisted they plan to go ahead with it as planned.
But the prospect of children in different parts of the country learning different spelling rules has led to calls for a final ruling on the matter by the Federal Constitutional Court.
The schoolbook publishers said they were considering whether they could sue for compensation if the reform finally collapsed.
